items.title: Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists
items.snippet: A mysterious particle overlooked for decades may hold the key to why matter survived the Big Bang, allowing stars, planets, and life to exist. Scientists believe this forgotten neutrino reshaped the early universe and may have left detectable gravitational wave signals that could help unlock the cosmos’s deepest mysteries.

items.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
items.snippet: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

items.title: This oddball reflective lava world is challenging to understand
items.snippet: Among Kepler and TESS's many surprising exoplanet discoveries are the ultra-short-period (USP) planets. These planets move very quickly and complete an orbit in less than 24 hours. Ancient astronomers thought that Mercury was so fast—it goes around the sun every 88 days—that they named it after the Roman god Mercury, who was the fast-traveling messenger of the gods. items.title: Looking for bats after dark can help science—and change how we see them
items.snippet: What's that chirping sound coming through the detector? Did you feel something whiz past? Those are just some ways people react when they encounter microbats for the first time. Microbats are small, mostly nocturnal mammals that use ultrasonic sounds to navigate and hunt at night. They do this through echolocation, producing calls and listening to the echoes that bounce back from objects and prey.

items.title: Giant virus yields potassium channel gene that illuminates complex protein evolution
items.snippet: Researchers have discovered a gene for a tandem potassium channel in an algal virus. The finding supports the view that giant viruses may have contributed significantly to the evolution of complex proteins. The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

items.title: Why do people prefer human empathy despite rating AI empathy higher?
items.snippet: More people are turning to artificial intelligence (AI)-powered chatbots for companionship and to address loneliness. But can AI-generated empathy replace human connection?

items.title: Chemists develop AI tool to convert human ingenuity into life-enhancing enzymes
items.snippet: Many have voiced concerns that artificial intelligence will take jobs away from humans. But assistant professor of chemistry Zhongyue (John) Yang, along with his former doctoral student Qianzhen Shao (now a postdoc at Stanford) and other team members, has created an AI tool that aims to elevate the work that scientists do—not replace them.

items.title: Calling species 'invasive'—and culling them—isn't done lightly. But it matters to Australia's threatened species
items.snippet: It may sound abstract, but distinctions between "native," "introduced" or "invasive" species can often be life or death. Species considered invasive in Australia—such as European rabbits and feral pigs—are often culled, while most native animals are generally left alone.

items.title: Ultracold atoms simulate hard-to-observe matter-antimatter pair production
items.snippet: According to quantum electrodynamics, the theory describing interactions between light and electrically charged particles, a sufficiently strong electric field can, in principle, convert some of its energy into particles and their antimatter partners. A particle's antimatter partner has the same mass and, for electrically charged particles, the opposite electric charge.

items.title: Hauntology examines how what happened in the past—and what didn't—informs the present
items.snippet: The spooky is a hugely popular phenomenon in British culture, demonstrated in what now seems like a month-long Halloween celebration, a rich tradition of horror cinema and a growing interest in the uncanny. But there are other manifestations of haunting.

items.title: How a 'tropical' shortcut could help particle collider experiments
items.snippet: Particle accelerators are expensive. Not just to build or to run, but also to predict the outcome of measurements obtained from them.

items.title: Novel chemical reaction expands options for building DNA-encoded libraries
items.snippet: Finding new drugs requires screening vast numbers of compounds to identify those that interact with a biological target. DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) help researchers explore these large collections by attaching a short DNA sequence to each molecule, acting as a molecular barcode that allows compounds with promising properties to be identified.
